claim: Sequence-specific DNA recognition underlies essential processes in gene regulation.
source: Sequence-specific DNA recognition underlies essential processes in gene regulation, yet methods for simultaneous predictions of genomic DNA recognition sites and their binding affinity remain lacking.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of DNA recognition in gene regulation, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Methods for simultaneous predictions of genomic DNA recognition sites and their binding affinity remain lacking.
source: Sequence-specific DNA recognition underlies essential processes in gene regulation, yet methods for simultaneous predictions of genomic DNA recognition sites and their binding affinity remain lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current methodologies, based on the authors' assessment of the field.

claim: IDEA is a residue-level, interpretable biophysical model capable of predicting binding sites and affinities of DNA-binding proteins.
source: Here, we present the Interpretable protein-DNA Energy Associative (IDEA) model, a residue-level, interpretable biophysical model capable of predicting binding sites and affinities of DNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model presented in the manuscript, representing the authors' characterization of their method.

claim: IDEA enables direct interpretation of physicochemical interactions among individual amino acids and nucleotides.
source: By fusing structures and sequences of known protein-DNA complexes into an optimized energy model, IDEA enables direct interpretation of physicochemical interactions among individual amino acids and nucleotides.
evidence: This describes a capability of the IDEA model based on its design and implementation.

claim: The IDEA energy model can accurately predict DNA recognition sites and their binding strengths across various protein families.
source: We demonstrate that this energy model can accurately predict DNA recognition sites and their binding strengths across various protein families.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation presented in the manuscript, including comparisons with experimental data.

claim: The IDEA model is integrated into a coarse-grained simulation framework that quantitatively captures the absolute protein-DNA binding free energies.
source: Additionally, the IDEA model is integrated into a coarse-grained simulation framework that quantitatively captures the absolute protein-DNA binding free energies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results presented in Figure 5 showing correlation with experimental binding free energies.

claim: Gene regulation guides important processes from development to disease response.
source: It guides important processes from development to disease response (Lee and Young, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lee and Young, 2013.

claim: Gene expression is tightly controlled by various DNA-binding proteins, including transcription factors (TFs) and epigenetic regulators.
source: Gene expression is tightly controlled by various DNA-binding proteins, including transcription factors (TFs) and epigenetic regulators (Orphanides and Reinberg, 2002; Ren et al., 2000; Jaenisch and Bird, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: TFs initiate gene expression by binding to specific DNA sequences, during which time a primary RNA transcript is synthesized from a gene's DNA.
source: TFs initiate gene expression by binding to specific DNA sequences, during which time a primary RNA transcript is synthesized from a gene's DNA (Latchman, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Latchman, 1997.

claim: Epigenetic regulators control gene expression by binding to specific chromatin regions, which spread post-translational modifications that modulate 3D genome organization.
source: On the other hand, epigenetic regulators control gene expression by binding to specific chromatin regions, which spread post-translational modifications that modulate 3D genome organization (Owen et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Owen et al., 2023.

claim: Characterizing the DNA-interaction specificities of DNA binding proteins is critical for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying many DNA-templated processes.
source: Therefore, characterizing the DNA-interaction specificities of DNA binding proteins is critical for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying many DNA-templated processes (Stormo and Zhao, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stormo and Zhao, 2010.

claim: Various experimental technologies have been developed and utilized to establish a comprehensive understanding of DNA binding processes.
source: To establish a comprehensive understanding of DNA binding processes, various experimental technologies have been developed and utilized (Solomon et al., 1988; Park, 2009; Bartlett et al., 2017; Berger and Bulyk, 2009; Meng et al., 2005; Maerkl and Quake, 2007; Fordyce et al., 2010; Ogawa and Biggin, 2012; Isakova et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental methods.

claim: ChIP-Seq, PBM, and SELEX have proven invaluable for measuring DNA-specific protein recognition.
source: These methods, such as Chromatin Immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-Seq; Solomon et al., 1988; Park, 2009; Furey, 2012), protein-binding microarray (PBM; Bulyk et al., 2001; Gordân et al., 2013; Afek et al., 2020), and systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX; Jolma et al., 2010; Ogawa and Biggin, 2012; Isakova et al., 2017), have proven invaluable for measuring DNA-specific protein recognition.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to these experimental methods.

claim: High-throughput measurement of large numbers of protein-DNA variants remains challenging due to the need for protein-specific antibodies, as well as the cost and intrinsic bias associated with these experiments.
source: Nonetheless, due to the need for protein-specific antibodies (Furey, 2012), as well as the cost and intrinsic bias associated with these experiments (Kohlberger and Gadermaier, 2022), high-throughput (HT) measurement of large numbers of protein-DNA variants remains challenging.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Furey, 2012 and Kohlberger and Gadermaier, 2022.

claim: Computational methods complement experimental efforts by providing the initial filter for assessing sequence-specific protein-DNA binding affinity.
source: Computational methods complement experimental efforts by providing the initial filter for assessing sequence-specific protein-DNA binding affinity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of computational methods in the field.

claim: Numerous methods have emerged to enable predictions of binding sites and affinities of DNA-binding proteins.
source: Numerous methods have emerged to enable predictions of binding sites and affinities of DNA-binding proteins (Weirauch et al., 2013; Alipanahi et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017; Rastogi et al., 2018; Roche et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2019; Rube et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to computational prediction methods.

claim: Many computational methods often utilized machine-learning-based training to extract sequence preference information from DNA or protein by utilizing experimental HT assays.
source: These methods often utilized machine-learning-based training to extract sequence preference information from DNA or protein by utilizing experimental HT assays (Weirauch et al., 2013; Alipanahi et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017; Rastogi et al., 2018; Rube et al., 2022), which rely on the availability and quality of experimental binding assays.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to machine learning methods.

claim: Many approaches employ deep neural networks, which could obscure the interpretation of interaction patterns governing protein-DNA binding specificities.
source: Additionally, many approaches employ deep neural networks (Roche et al., 2024; Liu and Tian, 2023; Nguyen et al., 2019), which could obscure the interpretation of interaction patterns governing protein-DNA binding specificities.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to deep learning methods and represents an inference about their interpretability limitations.

claim: Understanding interaction patterns is crucial for elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying various DNA-recognition processes, such as those seen in TFs.
source: Understanding these patterns, however, is crucial for elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying various DNA-recognition processes, such as those seen in TFs (Siggers and Gordân, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Siggers and Gordân, 2014.

claim: Over 5000 protein-DNA 3D structures, including TF-DNA complexes, have been published.
source: Nowadays, over 5000 protein-DNA 3D structures, including TF-DNA complexes, have been published (Mitra et al., 2025; Harini et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2025 and Harini et al., 2022.

claim: Protein-DNA 3D structures provide invaluable resources for understanding the physicochemical properties of protein-DNA binding patterns, extending beyond mere sequence information.
source: These data provide invaluable resources for understanding the physicochemical properties of protein-DNA binding patterns, extending beyond mere sequence information.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of structural data for understanding protein-DNA interactions.

claim: Emerging deep learning, probabilistic, and chemistry-based models are beginning to learn from protein-DNA co-crystal structures.
source: Emerging deep learning (Mitra et al., 2024), probabilistic (Wetzel et al., 2022), and chemistry-based models (Chiu et al., 2023) are beginning to learn from protein-DNA co-crystal structures.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent modeling approaches.

claim: Predictions from structure-based models are biophysically meaningful and can facilitate mechanistic understanding of molecular interactions.
source: Their predictions are biophysically meaningful and can facilitate mechanistic understanding of molecular interactions, thus holding great potential to guide experimental design and synthetic biology applications.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of structure-based predictions.

claim: The robustness of evolution provides an opportunity to extract the sequence-structure relationships embedded in existing complexes.
source: The very robustness of evolution (Bryngelson and Wolynes, 1987; Onuchic et al., 1997; Schafer et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2021) provides an opportunity to extract the sequence-structure relationships embedded in existing complexes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to evolutionary principles and represents an inference about their application.

claim: IDEA learns protein-DNA physicochemical interactions by fusing available biophysical structures and their associated sequences into an optimized energy model.
source: Here, we introduce the Interpretable protein-DNA Energy Associative (IDEA) model, a predictive model that learns protein-DNA physicochemical interactions by fusing available biophysical structures and their associated sequences into an optimized energy model (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology of IDEA as presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: IDEA can be used to accurately predict the sequence-specific DNA binding affinities of DNA-binding proteins.
source: We show that the model can be used to accurately predict the sequence-specific DNA binding affinities of DNA-binding proteins and is transferrable across the same protein superfamily.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the Results section showing correlations with experimental measurements.

claim: IDEA is transferrable across the same protein superfamily.
source: We show that the model can be used to accurately predict the sequence-specific DNA binding affinities of DNA-binding proteins and is transferrable across the same protein superfamily.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3 showing transferability within CATH superfamilies.

claim: The IDEA model can be enhanced by incorporating experimental binding data.
source: Moreover, the model can be enhanced by incorporating experimental binding data and can be generalized to enable base-pair resolution predictions of genomic DNA-binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing improved predictions when SELEX data is incorporated.

claim: IDEA can be generalized to enable base-pair resolution predictions of genomic DNA-binding sites.
source: Moreover, the model can be enhanced by incorporating experimental binding data and can be generalized to enable base-pair resolution predictions of genomic DNA-binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4 showing genomic binding site predictions.

claim: IDEA learns a family-specific interaction matrix that quantifies energetic interactions between each amino acid and nucleotide.
source: Notably, IDEA learns a family-specific interaction matrix that quantifies energetic interactions between each amino acid and nucleotide, allowing for a direct interpretation of the 'molecular grammar' governing sequence-specific protein-DNA binding affinities.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing the energy matrix.

claim: The IDEA energy model allows for a direct interpretation of the 'molecular grammar' governing sequence-specific protein-DNA binding affinities.
source: Notably, IDEA learns a family-specific interaction matrix that quantifies energetic interactions between each amino acid and nucleotide, allowing for a direct interpretation of the 'molecular grammar' governing sequence-specific protein-DNA binding affinities.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the interpretable energy matrices shown in the figures.

claim: The interpretable energy model is integrated into a simulation framework, enabling mechanistic studies of various biomolecular functions involving protein-DNA dynamics.
source: This interpretable energy model is further integrated into a simulation framework, enabling mechanistic studies of various biomolecular functions involving protein-DNA dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing simulation results.

claim: IDEA integrates both structures and corresponding sequences of known protein-DNA complexes to learn an interpretable energy model.
source: It integrates both structures and corresponding sequences of known protein-DNA complexes to learn an interpretable energy model based on the interacting amino acids and nucleotides at the protein-DNA binding interface.
evidence: This describes the methodology of IDEA.

claim: The IDEA model is trained using available protein-DNA complexes curated from existing databases.
source: The model is trained using available protein-DNA complexes curated from existing databases (Burley et al., 2023; Mitra et al., 2025).
evidence: This describes the data sources used for training, supported by citations.

claim: IDEA aims to learn a physicochemical-based energy model that quantitatively characterizes sequence-specific interactions between amino acids and nucleotides.
source: Unlike existing deep-learning-based protein-DNA binding prediction models, IDEA aims to learn a physicochemical-based energy model that quantitatively characterizes sequence-specific interactions between amino acids and nucleotides, thereby interpreting the 'molecular grammar' driving the binding energetics of protein-DNA interactions.
evidence: This describes the goal and approach of IDEA.

claim: The optimized IDEA energy model can be used to predict the binding affinity of any given protein-DNA pair based on its structures and sequences.
source: The optimized energy model can be used to predict the binding affinity of any given protein-DNA pair based on its structures and sequences.
evidence: This describes a capability of the trained model.

claim: The learned IDEA energy model can be incorporated into a simulation framework to study the dynamics of DNA-binding processes.
source: Finally, the learned energy model can be incorporated into a simulation framework to study the dynamics of DNA-binding processes, revealing mechanistic insights into various DNA-templated processes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 with simulation results.

claim: IDEA's de novo prediction based on one MAX crystal structure (PDB ID: 1HLO) correlates well with experimental values, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.67.
source: Our de novo prediction, based on one MAX crystal structure (PDB ID: 1HLO), correlates well with the experimental values (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.67) and correctly ranks the binding affinities of those DNA sequences (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.65, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 2A comparing predictions to experimental MITOMI data.

claim: IDEA's de novo prediction based on one MAX crystal structure correctly ranks the binding affinities of DNA sequences with a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.65.
source: Our de novo prediction, based on one MAX crystal structure (PDB ID: 1HLO), correlates well with the experimental values (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.67) and correctly ranks the binding affinities of those DNA sequences (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.65, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Including additional human-associated MAX-DNA complex structures and their associated sequences in the model training slightly improves the predictions.
source: Including additional human-associated MAX-DNA complex structures and their associated sequences in the model training slightly improves the predictions (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.68, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.65, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), albeit not significantly, likely due to the high structural similarity of the protein-DNA interfaces across all MAX proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The high structural similarity of the protein-DNA interfaces across all MAX proteins likely explains why including additional structures does not significantly improve predictions.
source: Including additional human-associated MAX-DNA complex structures and their associated sequences in the model training slightly improves the predictions (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.68, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.65, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), albeit not significantly, likely due to the high structural similarity of the protein-DNA interfaces across all MAX proteins.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors to explain the observation.

claim: When training the model with SELEX-seq data of MAX TF, IDEA showed a significant improvement in reproducing the MITOMI measurement with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.79.
source: Encouragingly, when training the model with the SELEX-seq data (Rastogi et al., 2018) of MAX TF, IDEA showed a significant improvement in reproducing the MITOMI measurement (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.79, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.76, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNA deoxycytidine (DC) exhibited strong interactions with protein arginine (R) in the MAX energy model.
source: Notably, DNA deoxycytidine (DC) exhibited strong interactions with protein arginine (R), consistent with the fact that the E-box region (CACGTG) frequently attracts the positively charged residues of bHLH TFs (Blackwell et al., 1990).
evidence: This is shown in the energy matrix in Figure 2B and supported by citation to Blackwell et al., 1990.

claim: The E-box region (CACGTG) frequently attracts the positively charged residues of bHLH TFs.
source: Notably, DNA deoxycytidine (DC) exhibited strong interactions with protein arginine (R), consistent with the fact that the E-box region (CACGTG) frequently attracts the positively charged residues of bHLH TFs (Blackwell et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Blackwell et al., 1990.

claim: Arginine was in close contact with deoxycytidine in the MAX crystal structure.
source: Importantly, arginine was in close contact with deoxycytidine in the crystal structure (Figure 2C), thus consistent with the strong DC-R interactions shown in the learned energy model.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The improved energy model shows additional unfavorable interactions between protein glutamic acid (E) and deoxycytidine, consistent with their negative charges.
source: Upon integrating the SELEX data into our model training, we found that the improved energy model shows additional unfavorable interactions between protein glutamic acid (E) and deoxycytidine, consistent with their negative charges (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and is consistent with known electrostatic principles.

claim: Including more experimental data can boost IDEA's predictive accuracy by refining the amino-acid-nucleotide interacting energy model to better align with physical principles.
source: Thus, including more experimental data can boost IDEA's predictive accuracy by refining the amino-acid-nucleotide interacting energy model to better align with physical principles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed improvements when SELEX data is incorporated.

claim: IDEA successfully differentiates strong from weak binders for 80% of the 22 proteins across 12 protein families, achieving AUC and balanced PRAUC scores greater than 0.5.
source: Our analysis shows that IDEA successfully differentiates strong from weak binders for 80% of the 22 proteins across 12 protein families, achieving AUC and balanced PRAUC scores greater than 0.5 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the AUC and PRAUC scores shown in the figures.

claim: IDEA demonstrates performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches including ProBound, DeepBind, rCLAMPS, and DBD-Hunter.
source: IDEA demonstrates performance comparable to these state-of-the-art approaches, and incorporating sequence features further improves its prediction accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 6; Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Incorporating sequence features further improves IDEA's prediction accuracy.
source: IDEA demonstrates performance comparable to these state-of-the-art approaches, and incorporating sequence features further improves its prediction accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 6; Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 comparing IDEA and IDEA-seq.

claim: IDEA outperforms a recent regression model that considers the shape of DNA with different sequences in 10-fold cross-validation.
source: We also performed 10-fold cross-validation on the binding affinities of protein-DNA pairs in this dataset and found that IDEA outperforms a recent regression model that considers the shape of DNA with different sequences (Yang et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: For PHO4, IDEA's predictions correlate well with experimental measurements, showing a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.60 and a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.63.
source: For PHO4, another bHLH TF, IDEA's predictions, trained on the only available protein-DNA structure (PDB ID: 1A0A), correlate well with experimental measurements, showing a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.60 and a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.63 (Figure 2—figure supplement 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Predictions on point-mutated sequences are known to be a challenging task due to their minor deviations from the wild-type sequence.
source: Predictions on point-mutated sequences are known to be a challenging task due to their minor deviations from the wild-type sequence.
evidence: This is a general statement about the difficulty of predicting point mutations, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: IDEA achieves accurate predictions for Zif268 point-mutated sequences, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.57 and a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.60.
source: Despite this, IDEA achieves accurate predictions, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.57 and a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.60 (Figure 2—figure supplement 8C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Incorporating additional training data from all available Zif268 structures from the same CATH zinc finger superfamily further improves the predictive accuracy to a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.63.
source: We further expanded the training dataset to include all available Zif268 structures and their associated sequences from the same CATH zinc finger superfamily (CATH ID: 3.30.160.60). Incorporating these additional training data further improves the predictive accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.63; Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.60, Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9.

claim: IDEA generally makes correct predictions of the binding affinity when trained on proteins that are homologous to MAX, with Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients larger than 0.5.
source: Our results show that IDEA generally makes correct predictions of the binding affinity when trained on proteins that are homologous to MAX, with Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients larger than 0.5 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the transferability analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The PHO4 protein (PDB ID: 1A0A) shares a highly similar DNA-binding interface with the MAX protein (PDB ID: 1HLO), despite sharing only a 33.41% probability of being homologous.
source: For example, the PHO4 protein (PDB ID: 1A0A) shares a highly similar DNA-binding interface with the MAX protein (PDB ID: 1HLO; Figure 3B), despite sharing only a 33.41% probability of being homologous.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural alignment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The energy model derived from the PHO4-DNA complex exhibits a similar amino-acid-nucleotide interactive pattern as that learned from the MAX-DNA complex.
source: Consequently, the energy model derived from the PHO4-DNA complex (Figure 3C) exhibits a similar amino-acid-nucleotide interactive pattern as that learned from the MAX-DNA complex (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the energy matrices in Figures 2B and 3C.

claim: Most of the energy models from the same protein family fall within the same cluster in PCA space.
source: Our analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) reveals that most of the energy models from the same protein family fall within the same cluster, while those from different protein families exhibit distinct patterns.
evidence: This is shown in the PCA analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative distance between energy models in PCA space reflects the degree of transferability between them.
source: Moreover, the relative distance between energy models in PCA space reflects the degree of transferability between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA analysis and transferability results.

claim: Multiple techniques have been developed to enable HT mapping of genomic protein-DNA binding locations, such as ChIP-seq, DAP-seq, and FAIRE-seq.
source: Although multiple techniques have been developed to enable HT mapping of genomic protein-DNA binding locations, such as ChIP-seq (Park, 2009; Furey, 2012; de Souza, 2012), DAP-seq (Bartlett et al., 2017), and FAIRE-seq (Giresi et al., 2007), challenges remain for precisely pinpointing protein-binding sites at a base-pair resolution.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to these experimental techniques.

claim: Challenges remain for precisely pinpointing protein-binding sites at a base-pair resolution.
source: Although multiple techniques have been developed to enable HT mapping of genomic protein-DNA binding locations, such as ChIP-seq (Park, 2009; Furey, 2012; de Souza, 2012), DAP-seq (Bartlett et al., 2017), and FAIRE-seq (Giresi et al., 2007), challenges remain for precisely pinpointing protein-binding sites at a base-pair resolution.
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations of current experimental techniques.

claim: The applicability of genomic mapping techniques for different DNA-binding proteins is restricted by the quality of antibody designs.
source: Furthermore, the applicability of these techniques for different DNA-binding proteins is restricted by the quality of antibody designs (Furey, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furey, 2012.

claim: A predictive computational framework would significantly reduce the costs and accelerate the identification of genomic binding sites of DNA-binding proteins.
source: Therefore, a predictive computational framework would significantly reduce the costs and accelerate the identification of genomic binding sites of DNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential benefits of computational prediction methods.

claim: IDEA's prediction successfully identifies the majority of the MAX binding sites, achieving an AUC score of 0.81.
source: Our prediction successfully identifies the majority of the MAX binding sites, achieving an AUC score of 0.81 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ROC analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IDEA successfully identified genomic binding sites for two additional typical DNA-binding proteins.
source: We also tested IDEA's predictive performance on two additional typical DNA-binding proteins and successfully identified their genomic binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing predictions for EGR1 and CTCF.

claim: IDEA provides an accurate initial prediction of genomic recognition sites of DNA-binding proteins based only on DNA sequences.
source: Therefore, IDEA provides an accurate initial prediction of genomic recognition sites of DNA-binding proteins based only on DNA sequences, facilitating more focused experimental efforts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic binding site prediction results.

claim: IDEA holds the potential to identify binding sites beyond the experimental resolution.
source: Furthermore, IDEA holds the potential to identify binding sites beyond the experimental resolution and can aid in the interpretation of other sequencing techniques to uncover additional factors that influence genome-wide DNA binding, such as chromatin accessibility (Boyle et al., 2008; Corces et al., 2017; Granja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future potential applications, supported by citations to relevant techniques.

claim: Coarse-grained protein-nucleic acid models have shown strong advantages in investigating large biomolecular systems.
source: Coarse-grained protein-nucleic acid models have shown strong advantages in investigating large biomolecular systems (Savelyev and Papoian, 2010; Davtyan et al., 2012; Bascom and Schlick, 2018; Tan and Takada, 2020; Chakraborty et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to coarse-grained modeling studies.

claim: The structure-based protein model and 3-Site-Per-Nucleotide (3SPN) DNA model have been developed at the residue resolution to enable efficient sampling of biomolecular systems involving protein and DNA.
source: Notably, the structure-based protein model (Clementi et al., 2000) and 3-Site-Per-Nucleotide (3SPN) DNA model Freeman et al., 2014a have been developed at the residue resolution to enable efficient sampling of biomolecular systems involving protein and DNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to these modeling approaches.

claim: A combination of structure-based protein model and 3SPN DNA model has proved instrumental in quantitatively studying multiple large chromatin systems.
source: A combination of these two models has proved instrumental in quantitatively studying multiple large chromatin systems (Lin et al., 2021c), including nucleosomal DNA unwrapping (Zhang et al., 2016; Lequieu et al., 2016; Parsons and Zhang, 2019), interactions between nucleosomes (Moller et al., 2019; Lin and Zhang, 2024), large chromatin organizations (Ding et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Lin and Zhang, 2024), and its modulation by chromatin factors (Watanabe et al., 2018; Leicher et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to chromatin modeling studies.

claim: The non-bonded interactions between protein and DNA in previous models were primarily guided by Debye-Hückel treatment of electrostatic interactions, which did not consider sequence-specific interactions between individual protein amino acids and DNA nucleotides.
source: Although both the protein and DNA force fields have been systematically optimized (Noel et al., 2016; Knotts et al., 2007; Hinckley et al., 2013; Freeman et al., 2014a; Freeman et al., 2014b), the non-bonded interactions between protein and DNA were primarily guided by Debye-Hückel treatment of electrostatic interactions, which did not consider sequence-specific interactions between individual protein amino acids and DNA nucleotides.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous models, supported by citations to force field development.

claim: Upon incorporating the learned energy model into the simulation model and computing protein-DNA binding free energies through umbrella sampling, a significant improvement in predictive accuracy was observed.
source: However, upon incorporating the learned energy model into our simulation model and computing protein-DNA binding free energies through umbrella sampling (Torrie and Valleau, 1977; Figure 5B), we observed a significant improvement in predictive accuracy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the improved correlation shown in Figure 5C compared to Figure 5A.

claim: The predicted binding free energies from IDEA-based simulations correlate strongly with experimental measurements with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.81 and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.90.
source: The predicted binding free energies (Kumar et al., 1992; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) from our simulations correlate strongly with experimental measurements (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.81; Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.90) and near-perfectly reproduce the experimental binding affinities (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The IDEA-based simulation represents a substantial improvement over the previous model with non-sequence-specific homogeneous electrostatic interactions.
source: This prediction also represents a substantial improvement over the previous model, which depicts protein-DNA interactions through non-sequence-specific homogeneous electrostatic interactions (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.60, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.70; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the correlations in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Due to an undetermined prefactor in the IDEA training, it can only provide relative binding free energies in reduced units for different protein-DNA complexes.
source: Notably, due to an undetermined prefactor in the IDEA training, it can only provide relative binding free energies in reduced units for different protein-DNA complexes.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the IDEA energy model.

claim: The IDEA-incorporated simulation model can predict the absolute binding free energies with physical units.
source: In contrast, the IDEA-incorporated simulation model can predict the absolute binding free energies with physical units.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C showing predictions in kcal/mol units.

claim: IDEA achieves accurate de novo prediction using only a few protein-DNA complexes within the same protein superfamily.
source: By leveraging the sequence-structure relationship inherent in protein-DNA complex structures, IDEA achieves accurate de novo prediction using only a few protein-DNA complexes within the same protein superfamily.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transferability results in Figure 3.

claim: IDEA enables predictions of genomic binding sites and shows good agreement with the ChIP-seq measurements.
source: In addition, despite the complicated in vivo environment, IDEA enables predictions of genomic binding sites and shows good agreement with the ChIP-seq measurements (Figures 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 showing correlation with ChIP-seq data.

claim: IDEA features rapid prediction, typically requiring 1–3 days to predict base-pair resolution genomic binding sites of a 1 Mb DNA region using a single CPU.
source: Moreover, IDEA features rapid prediction, typically requiring 1–3 days to predict base-pair resolution genomic binding sites of a 1 Mb DNA region using a single CPU.
evidence: This describes the computational efficiency of IDEA.

claim: IDEA's prediction can be trivially parallelized, making it possible to perform genome-wide predictions of DNA recognition sites by a given protein within weeks.
source: Furthermore, IDEA's prediction can be trivially parallelized, making it possible to perform genome-wide predictions of DNA recognition sites by a given protein within weeks.
